title: World Geography · Episode 2
chapters: Caves: the hidden world beneath our feet
Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre: Australia's sometimes sea
Uluru and Kata Tjuta: the rocks at the heart of Australia

units.t: World Geography. Episode two.
In this episode: Caves: the hidden world beneath our feet, Deserts, Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre: Australia's sometimes sea and Uluru and Kata Tjuta: the rocks at the heart of Australia.
Part one. Caves: the hidden world beneath our feet.
Under quiet paddocks and plains lie vast cave systems, sculpted drop by drop over hundreds of thousands of years.
Here is how rain dissolves rock, and what caves preserve.
Rain that eats rock.
Drive across the Nullarbor Plain and you see almost nothing: a flat, treeless expanse.
The name comes from the Latin for 'no tree'.
Yet beneath it lies one of the largest areas of limestone on Earth, riddled with caves, some holding long underground lakes explored by divers.
Such landscapes are called karst, after a limestone region in Slovenia.
Most caves are made by dissolving rock.
Rain absorbs a little carbon dioxide from the air, and much more as it soaks through soil full of decaying plants.
This forms a weak carbonic acid, the same acid that fizzes in soft drinks.
It slowly dissolves limestone, widening cracks over tens to hundreds of thousands of years into passages and chambers.
When the water table drops, air fills the passages.
Stalactites and stalagmites.
Once a cave fills with air, a new kind of sculpture begins.
Water dripping from the ceiling carries dissolved limestone.
When it reaches the cave air, it releases some of its carbon dioxide, and a tiny amount of the mineral calcite is left behind.
Drip by drip, a thin hollow straw forms, which can thicken into an icicle-like stalactite hanging from the roof.
Where drops land, calcite builds upward into a stalagmite.
A memory aid: stalactites hold 'tight' to the ceiling, while stalagmites 'might' reach up one day.
When the two meet they form a column.
Growth is usually a fraction of a millimetre a year, so touching formations is discouraged because skin oils can stop them growing.
Australia's great caves.
Australia's best-known show caves are the Jenolan Caves in New South Wales, where visitors have explored lit chambers since the 1800s.
Scientific dating suggests the caves are very old, possibly hundreds of millions of years, making them among the oldest known open caves in the world.
In South Australia, the Naracoorte Caves act as natural traps.
For hundreds of thousands of years animals fell through openings in the ground and could not climb out, leaving a remarkable fossil record that includes Australia's extinct megafauna.
With Riversleigh in Queensland, Naracoorte was World Heritage listed in 1994.
In north Queensland, the Undara lava tubes are a different kind of cave, formed by flowing lava rather than water.
Sinkholes and giants.
As caves grow, their roofs can thin and collapse, opening a hole called a sinkhole or doline.
Some form slowly as the ground sags.
Others appear suddenly, swallowing roads, cars and occasionally buildings.
Mount Gambier in South Australia is famous for its water-filled sinkholes, including the Umpherston Sinkhole's sunken garden.
On Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula, sinkholes called cenotes open into water-filled caves.
The ancient Maya relied on them for fresh water, and some were sacred places for offerings.
Divers explore flooded passages linking them that stretch for hundreds of kilometres.
Caves also set records.
Mammoth Cave in Kentucky is the longest known system, with more than 600 kilometres of mapped passages.
Vietnam's Son Doong is so vast that parts of its main passage could hold city buildings, and a jungle grows where the roof has collapsed.
Life in the dark.
Deep caves are dark, damp and short of food, yet life has moved in.
Over many generations, many cave animals have lost their eyes and pigment, since neither helps in total darkness, and developed long antennae or legs and sharp senses of touch and smell.
The olm, a pale salamander from the caves of south-eastern Europe, can live for many decades and survive for years without eating.
Australia has its own hidden cave fauna, including blind fish and shrimp in the underground waters of Cape Range in Western Australia.
Caves also preserve climate records in their formations, helping scientists read the past.
Many remain unexplored, and volunteers are still finding new passages around the world, including in Australia.
They are fragile places worth protecting.
The key idea: Slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolves limestone, opening up caves over hundreds of thousands of years.
Part two. Deserts.
The biggest desert on Earth is covered in ice.
Deserts are defined by thirst, not heat, and they are far more alive than they look.
Dry, not hot.
Geographers define deserts by dryness, not heat.
A common rule of thumb is less than about 250 millimetres of rain or snow a year, though a better measure compares rainfall with how much water could evaporate.
Slightly wetter land, around 250 to 500 millimetres, is semi-arid.
Together, arid and semi-arid land covers roughly a third of Earth's land.
With little moisture or cloud to trap heat, desert nights can be cold even after scorching days.
By this definition the largest desert is Antarctica, about 14 million square kilometres.
Much of its interior receives less than 50 millimetres of precipitation a year, as melted water.
The ice is kilometres thick because snow almost never melts.
The Arctic ranks second.
The McMurdo Dry Valleys, largely free of ice, resemble Mars.
Why deserts form.
Several forces make deserts.
The biggest is global air circulation: warm, moist air rises near the equator, drops its rain, then sinks as dry air around 30 degrees north and south.
That belt holds the Sahara, the Arabian, the Kalahari and much of inland Australia.
Rain shadows form where mountains wring moisture from air on one side, as in Patagonia.
Some deserts, like the Gobi, are too far from the sea for moist air to reach.
The Atacama in Chile and the Namib in southern Africa lie beside cold ocean currents that chill the air and stop rain clouds forming.
Climate can change.
The Sahara, the largest hot desert at about 9 million square kilometres, was green between roughly 11,000 and 5,000 years ago, with lakes, hippos and crocodiles.
Australia's deserts.
Geoscience Australia lists ten named deserts covering about 18% of the mainland, and around 70% of the continent is arid or semi-arid.
The largest is the Great Victoria Desert, spanning Western Australia and South Australia.
Others include the Great Sandy, Tanami, Gibson and Simpson.
The Simpson Desert is known for its long, parallel red sand dunes, some running well over 100 kilometres.
Much of the interior drains towards Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre, Australia's lowest point at about 15 metres below sea level.
The lake is usually a salt crust, filling completely only a few times a century.
When it does, huge numbers of waterbirds arrive to breed.
Life in the desert.
Cacti and many succulents store water in thick stems or leaves.
Australia's spinifex forms tough hummocks that shelter small animals.
After rare heavy rain, dormant seeds flower and finish their life cycle in weeks.
The thorny devil, a small Australian lizard, has grooves between its scales that draw water by capillary action to its mouth, so it can drink from damp sand or dew.
Many desert animals are active only at night.
Camel humps hold fat, not water; camels simply tolerate dehydration and conserve water extremely well.
Aboriginal peoples, including the many language groups of the Western Desert, have lived in arid country for tens of thousands of years.
Survival depended on knowledge of rock holes, soaks and seasonal plants, passed on through song, story and ceremony.
Travelling in dry country.
Australia's deserts are beautiful and increasingly visited, but they punish poor preparation.
Fuel and water can be hundreds of kilometres apart, phone coverage disappears quickly and summer temperatures can pass 45 degrees.
Carry far more water than you expect to need, commonly several litres per person per day plus extra for emergencies.
Check road conditions, since dirt roads close after rain, and some remote tracks need permits, including to cross Aboriginal land.
Tell someone your route and expected arrival.
Carry a personal locator beacon or satellite device.
If you break down, stay with your vehicle.
It gives shade and is far easier for searchers to spot than a person walking.
The key idea: A desert is defined by very low rainfall, not temperature, which is why Antarctica is the world's largest desert.
Part three. Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre: Australia's sometimes sea.
For most of its life it is a blinding sheet of salt.
Then, every so often, distant floods turn it into Australia's largest lake and birds arrive from hundreds of kilometres away.
Australia's lowest point.
In the arid north of South Australia lies Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre, the lowest natural point on the Australian continent, about 15 metres below sea level.
Kati Thanda comes from the Arabana people, the traditional owners, for whom the lake holds deep cultural significance.
The dual name was formally adopted in 2012.
Lake Eyre honours the English-born explorer Edward John Eyre, who saw parts of it in 1840.
Most of the time the lake is dry, a vast flat crust of salt that glares white under the sun.
It has two main parts, Lake Eyre North, much the larger, and Lake Eyre South, joined by a narrow channel.
A continental drain.
Water flows downhill, and in central Australia much of it flows towards Kati Thanda.
Its catchment, the Lake Eyre Basin, covers about 1.
2 million square kilometres, roughly one sixth of Australia, across parts of Queensland, the Northern Territory, South Australia and New South Wales.
It is one of the largest internally draining basins in the world, meaning none of its water ever reaches the sea.
Rivers such as the Diamantina, the Georgina and Cooper Creek wander slowly across a vast, flat landscape known as the Channel Country.
Floodwater can take months to travel from Queensland to the lake, and most of it evaporates or soaks into the ground on the way.
When the water comes.
The basin is so dry and evaporation so intense that it takes exceptional rain to deliver serious water to Kati Thanda.
Small floods reach the lake fairly often, and a significant filling happens only every several years.
Filling close to capacity happens only a few times in a century.
The great floods of the 1950s and 1974 were among the biggest on record.
When full, it is the largest lake in Australia, covering around 9,500 square kilometres.
Even then it is mostly just a few metres deep.
As the water spreads over the salt crust, it dissolves salt and turns saltier, and the shallow water can glow pink from salt-loving algae and microbes.
An explosion of life.
When water arrives, the desert erupts with life.
Eggs of tiny crustaceans such as brine shrimp, dormant in the dry mud, hatch within days.
Fish washed down the rivers multiply in the fresher water.
Then the birds come.
Pelicans, silver gulls, terns, ducks and other waterbirds arrive in huge numbers, many to breed on islands in the lake.
Australian pelicans appear to fly hundreds of kilometres from the coast, and exactly how they detect that the lake has filled remains a mystery.
Breeding is a race against time.
As the lake shrinks and salt rises, fish die off and food runs out, and colonies may be abandoned before all the chicks fledge.
A record on the salt.
In 1964 British driver Donald Campbell brought his jet-turbine car, Bluebird CN7, to Lake Eyre.
Unusual rain softened the salt and delayed his runs for weeks.
On 17 July 1964, on a surface still damp, he set a land speed record of about 648 kilometres per hour, 403 miles per hour.
Later that year he set a water speed record in Western Australia, the only person to break both records in a year.
The basin itself is one of the largest unregulated dryland river systems left on Earth, flowing in irregular boom and bust cycles that drive fish breeding and green the Channel Country pastures.
Scientists, pastoralists and Aboriginal communities who have cared for it for tens of thousands of years work to protect it.
The key idea: Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre lies about 15 metres below sea level in outback South Australia and is usually a dry salt crust.
Part four. Uluru and Kata Tjuta: the rocks at the heart of Australia.
A single rock rising out of a flat red plain looks like it was dropped from the sky.
The real story involves vanished mountains, half a billion years and a culture that has known this place for tens of thousands of years.
A rock that glows red.
Stand on the plain at sunset and Uluru seems to catch fire, shifting from ochre to orange to deep red, then purple.
It rises about 348 metres, higher than the Eiffel Tower, in the south of the Northern Territory, about 450 kilometres by road from Alice Springs.
It is striking because the land around is almost flat, covered in red sand, spinifex and desert oaks.
The base walk is roughly ten kilometres and takes most people about three hours.
The red is only a thin skin.
Inside, the rock is dull grey.
Its iron-bearing minerals oxidise in air and rain, so the surface has rusted.
The low sun at dawn and dusk scatters away blue light, leaving warm reds.
After rare heavy rain, Uluru turns silvery and waterfalls pour down its gullies.
Vanished mountains, tipped layers.
More than 500 million years ago, a mountain range in central Australia was being worn down.
Rivers dumped the debris in great fans of sand and gravel, which a shallow sea buried.
The weight pressed the grains into solid rock.
The coarse sand became Uluru's sandstone, rich in feldspar.
The faint parallel lines up Uluru's sides are the original sand layers, which should lie flat.
Hundreds of millions of years ago, movements of the crust squeezed central Australia and tilted Uluru's layers by close to 90 degrees.
Erosion then stripped away the softer rock around the tougher stone.
Geologists think much of Uluru continues underground, so what we see may be only a fraction of the whole.
Kata Tjuta, many heads.
Kata Tjuta, once called the Olgas, lies about 30 kilometres west of Uluru.
The pebbles and boulders from the same ancient mountains became its conglomerate, so the two are siblings, sorted by the rivers into different sizes of stone.
Many visitors are surprised that it is taller: its highest dome rises around 546 metres above the plain.
Kata Tjuta means 'many heads' in the local language, and there are 36 rounded domes separated by deep valleys and narrow gorges.
Conglomerate, a jumble of pebbles and boulders cemented together, weathers differently from sandstone, which is why it has broken into many separate shapes.
The Valley of the Winds walk winds between the domes, where the temperature drops and sounds echo strangely.
The Anangu and Tjukurpa.
Long before any geologist arrived, the Anangu knew this country intimately.
Anangu are the Traditional Owners, and Aboriginal people have lived in central Australia for many tens of thousands of years.
For Anangu, the landscape is explained through Tjukurpa, a body of law, knowledge and story that describes how ancestral beings travelled across the land and created its features.
Marks, caves and waterholes around Uluru are linked to these stories and to rules for living.
Some places are sacred and are not to be photographed or visited by outsiders, which is why certain parts of the base walk carry signs asking visitors to respect them.
To Anangu, Uluru is not a scenic backdrop.
Names, handback and the climb.
In 1873 the explorer William Gosse saw the rock and named it Ayers Rock after Sir Henry Ayers, a South Australian politician.
For about a century tourism grew, and many visitors climbed a steep route up one side, despite Anangu asking people not to.
On 26 October 1985 ownership of the national park was formally handed back to Anangu, who leased it to the federal government for joint management.
The park is World Heritage listed for both natural and cultural values, and the Anangu name Uluru now comes first in official use.
After years of discussion, the park board decided to end the climb, and it closed permanently on 26 October 2019, exactly 34 years after the handback.
The key idea: Uluru is a huge, isolated sandstone monolith whose red colour is only a thin coat of rust.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Which acid is mainly responsible for dissolving limestone to form caves?
Answer. Carbonic acid.
Question two. What mainly defines a desert?
Answer. Very low rainfall compared with evaporation.
Question three. Roughly how far below sea level is the lowest part of Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre?
Answer. About 15 metres.
Question four. What gives Uluru its red colour?
Answer. A thin coating of oxidised iron.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
